subject: Animal abundance model from replicate counts to estimate detection probability

messages.author: 74f2e6fef4c447fd
messages.subject: Animal abundance model from replicate counts to estimate detection probability
parts:
Hi INLA folks,

I imagine this question has been asked before, but I have searched and can't find an answer. So here goes.

Wildlife biologists commonly use so-called 'N-Mixture' models to estimate animal abundance.  Sampling involves going to multiple sites in a study area, visiting each site, say, three times in short succession.   The purpose of the replicate counts per site is to quantify detection probability, so that this probability can be used to correct abundance estimates for imperfect detection. Estimates are otherwise biased low, and using zero-inflated models doesn't always help.  Both counts and detection probability are often modeled with covariates.  These models are often evaluated using BUGS and they look like this:

    # Ecological model for true abundance
    for (i in 1:R){
      N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
      log(lambda[i]) <- alpha0 + alpha1 * X[i]
      # Observation model for replicated counts
      for (j in 1:T){
        y[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])
        p[i,j] <- exp(lp[i,j])/(1+exp(lp[i,j]))
        lp[i,j] <- beta0 + beta1 * X[i]
      } #j
    } #i

Is there a way to evaluate this type of model using INLA?  I suspect there might be, using 'copy' or 'replicate', or specifying multiple distributions like 'c(binomial, poisson)', but I am not clever enough to figure this out. If this could be done in INLA, it would make model evaluation A LOT quicker and allow convenient ways to code spatiotemporal random effects.

I have attached code to simulate data and analyze it using OpenBugs, in case that is helpful.

Thanks,
Tim

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Animal abundance model from replicate counts to estimate detection probability
parts:
On Mon, 2016-12-12 at 15:23 -0800, TDM wrote:
> en evaluated using BUGS and they
> look like this:
>
>     # Ecological model for true abundance
>     for (i in 1:R){
>       N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
>       log(lambda[i]) <- alpha0 + alpha1 * X[i]
>       # Observation model for replicated counts
>       for (j in 1:T){
>         y[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])
>         p[i,j] <- exp(lp[i,j])/(1+exp(lp[i,j]))
>         lp[i,j] <- beta0 + beta1 * X[i]
>       } #j
>     } #i

Hi

even if we integrate out N[i], there are in general two linear
predictors involved, one for N[i] and then one for y[i,j]. One of the
fundamental assumptions in the code is that each response depends on
only one linear predictor [this is a code assumption and also
simplifies some of the computations], so we cannot do that model.

If N[i] is fixed, then its ok.  

if you *know* that the dependence in N[i] is as described, and as
simple as this, then its possible with additional coding. Maybe we
could discuss this issue off-list.


Best
H





--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org
